In a 'cards' section, a list item that starts with a link or a **bold name** and then a colon becomes an organization card.

sections.label: Content note
sections.body: **Content note:** this page discusses abuse, neglect, the drugging of residents and deaths in nursing homes. [Where to report abuse is listed below.](#kop-ri-report)

sections.label: Not the TTI
sections.heading: Not the troubled teen industry
sections.body:
Nursing homes are not part of the troubled teen industry, and Kids Over Profits does not track nursing homes or assisted living facilities.

They are on this site for the same reason youth programs are: people who cannot leave are held in a facility, out of sight, and mistreated there, and their care is run as a business. Some of the same investors have owned both nursing homes and youth programs.

We are not experts on long-term care. Residents, their families, ombudsmen and the organizations listed below have done this work for decades.

sections.label: Residents who cannot leave
sections.heading: Residents who cannot leave
sections.body:
A nursing home resident who needs help to eat, wash or walk cannot leave, and many residents with dementia live in locked units. Their safety depends on the staff who hold them.

The old and the young were once confined together. For centuries elderly, sick and disabled people and poor children were held in the same workhouses and almshouses ([orphan care timeline](/orphanages/)). In the United States, Dorothea Dix investigated almshouses and jails from 1841 into the 1880s and found children, elderly people and people with mental illness confined together, and the children neglected, unschooled and exposed to physical and sexual abuse. Reformers moved the children out: New York's Children's Law of 1875 barred children aged 3 to 16 from county poorhouses, and disabled children went to institutions of their own, which became one of the roots of the troubled teen industry ([how the threads met](/birth-of-the-tti/)).

The harms are the same in both today. Federal rules have to spell out a resident's right to be free from "corporal punishment, involuntary seclusion" and from "any physical or chemical restraint not required to treat the resident's medical symptoms," and bar restraints imposed "for purposes of discipline or convenience."[^1] The rules are broken anyway. Nursing home deficiencies for abuse rose from 430 in 2013 to 875 in 2017, with the largest increase among the most severe, and staff were the abusers more often than anyone else.[^2]

sections.label: Run for profit
sections.heading: Run for profit
sections.body:
Most nursing homes are businesses, and most of their money is public. That combination built the youth residential industry too: after Medicaid and Medicare were created in 1965, public money could follow a child into a private placement, and Devereux's leaders told the Senate Finance Committee that 95 percent of its residential treatment revenue came from Medicaid ([our summary of the 2024 report](/warehouses-of-neglect/)).

Table: Nursing homes and assisted living
| Measure | Figure |
|---|---|
| Nursing homes certified by CMS, July 2025 | 14,742[^3] |
| People living in them | About 1.24 million[^3] |
| For-profit, nonprofit and government-owned, 2025 | 73, 20 and 7 percent[^4] |
| Owned by private equity, 2022 (GAO estimate) | About 5 percent; federal data cannot show the full number[^3] |
| Residents whose main payer is Medicaid / Medicare | 63 percent / 14 percent[^3] |
| Nursing care per resident per day | 3.85 hours, most of it from nurse aides[^3] |
| Homes cited for deficiencies that harmed residents or put them in immediate jeopardy | 27 percent[^3] |
| Assisted living communities, 2022 | About 32,200, with 988,800 residents; 81.5 percent for-profit[^5] |

When private equity buys a nursing home, more residents die. A study of Medicare patients found that a private equity buyout raised a nursing home's patient mortality by about 11 percent; nurse staffing fell after the buyouts, which the authors name as one reason for the deaths.[^6] The private equity owners of care providers make each facility a separate legal entity, which limits the investors' liability, and load companies with debt to pay shareholders, which pushes facilities to cut staff ([corporatization timeline](/corporatization/)).

sections.label: The same investors
sections.heading: The same investors
sections.body:
The Carlyle Group and Onex have each owned a nursing home chain and a youth program company. Carlyle owned HCR ManorCare, one of the largest nursing home chains, from 2007[^7] until ManorCare went bankrupt in 2018 owing $7.1 billion,[^8][^9] and had invested in Newport Academy by 2017.[^10] It sold Newport to Onex, which bought a majority of Newport Healthcare in 2021 ([corporatization timeline](/corporatization/)).[^11]

Onex had owned both kinds of company before. In 2005 it bought Skilled Healthcare Group, then the operator of 70 nursing and assisted living homes in California, Texas, Nevada and Kansas;[^12] Skilled Healthcare merged into Genesis HealthCare in 2015.[^13] Onex took a stake in ResCare in 2004 and bought the rest in 2010.[^14] ResCare's filings describe residential treatment facilities, group homes and foster care for "young people with emotional and behavioral issues" and "juveniles in the justice system."[^15] ResCare was renamed BrightSpring Health in 2018;[^16] two West Virginia programs under the ResCare name are in our records.

Real estate investment trusts such as Sabra and CareTrust own nursing homes and have moved into adult addiction treatment.[^17] We did not find a trust or private equity firm we could document owning both nursing homes and youth residential programs today. If you know of one, please tell us.

sections.label: Drugged into compliance
sections.heading: Drugged into compliance
sections.body:
Giving a drug to make a person easier to manage, not to treat a condition, is chemical restraint. Human Rights Watch found in 2018 that in an average week, nursing homes gave antipsychotics to over 179,000 people without a diagnosis the drugs are approved for, often without free and informed consent, for staff convenience or to discipline residents.[^18]

When regulators pushed back, the homes changed the paperwork. CMS's National Partnership to Improve Dementia Care, started in 2012, cut the reported rate of antipsychotic use among long-stay residents from 23.9 to 15.7 percent by early 2017.[^19] That measure leaves out residents diagnosed with schizophrenia, and in 2026 the HHS Inspector General, reviewing inspections of 40 nursing homes, found medical directors making inappropriate schizophrenia diagnoses to justify antipsychotics and get around Medicare safeguards.[^20] The Senate Finance Committee documented the same chemical restraint in youth residential treatment run by Universal Health Services, Acadia Healthcare, Devereux and Vivant in 2024 ([our summary](/warehouses-of-neglect/)).[^21]

sections.label: Oversight that misses it
sections.heading: Oversight that misses it
sections.body:
Abuse goes unreported. The HHS Inspector General estimated that one in five high-risk emergency room claims for nursing home residents in 2016 came from potential abuse or neglect, and that nursing homes failed to report many of these incidents to the state as federal rules require.[^22] CMS did not check whether state agencies referred abuse cases to law enforcement.[^2]

Families are kept from what is known. State agencies inspect nursing homes for CMS and publish the results on Care Compare,[^23] but until 2019 the roughly 400 homes that qualified for CMS's Special Focus Facility program for the worst records, and were not given one of its limited places, were kept from the public.[^24] Until June 2023 Care Compare did not show which homes shared an owner or how that owner's other homes performed.[^25] For assisted living the gaps are wider: in 2018, 26 state Medicaid agencies could not say how many critical incidents, such as abuse or unexplained deaths, happened in the assisted living facilities they paid for.[^26]

Courts can be closed to residents too. Homes may ask residents to sign arbitration agreements that send disputes to a private arbitrator instead of a court; a 2019 federal rule allows them but bars making them a condition of admission or of continued care.[^27]

sections.label: Younger disabled people
sections.heading: Younger disabled people
sections.body: In *Olmstead v. L.C.* (1999) the Supreme Court held that the unjustified segregation of people with disabilities violates the Americans with Disabilities Act.[^28] Nursing homes still house many disabled people under 65. They are more likely than older residents to live in for-profit and lower-quality homes, and in many states the rate at which younger people are placed stayed flat or grew while it fell for older adults.[^29] We have not found figures on how many young people move from youth programs into nursing homes.

sections.label: Where to report abuse
sections.heading: Where to report abuse
sections.body:
- **If someone is in danger now**, call 911.
- **Long-Term Care Ombudsman.** Every state has one. Ombudsmen take complaints from nursing home and assisted living residents and their families, and work for the resident. Find yours through the Eldercare Locator, 1-800-677-1116, or [Consumer Voice's directory](https://theconsumervoice.org/get-help/).
- **State survey agency.** Complaints about abuse, neglect, too few staff or unsafe conditions in a nursing home go to the state survey agency, usually part of the state health department. CMS lists [each state's agency](https://www.cms.gov/medicare/health-safety-standards/quality-safety-oversight-general-information/contact-information), or call 1-800-MEDICARE, 1-800-633-4227 (TTY 1-877-486-2048), for the contact.
- **Adult Protective Services** takes reports of abuse, neglect and exploitation of older and disabled adults. Find your state's number through [NAPSA](https://www.napsa-now.org/help-in-your-area/).
- **Medicaid Fraud Control Units** investigate and prosecute [abuse and neglect of residents](https://oig.hhs.gov/fraud/medicaid-fraud-control-units-mfcu/) in facilities that take Medicaid.
- **Protection and Advocacy.** For disabled residents, including younger people who want to leave a nursing home, there is a [Protection and Advocacy agency](https://www.ndrn.org/about/ndrn-member-agencies/) in every state and territory.
- **988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline**, 24 hours: call or text [988](tel:988).

For abuse in a youth program, see [our reporting directory](/report-abuse/).

sections.label: Organizations to learn from
sections.heading: Learn from the people who work on this
sections.body:
- [National Consumer Voice for Quality Long-Term Care](https://theconsumervoice.org/): Founded in 1975 as the National Citizens' Coalition for Nursing Home Reform; speaks for long-term care residents nationally and runs the National Long-Term Care Ombudsman Resource Center.
- [Long Term Care Community Coalition (nursinghome411)](https://nursinghome411.org/): Publishes nursing home staffing, inspection and antipsychotic data and guides for residents and families.
- [Center for Medicare Advocacy](https://medicareadvocacy.org/): A nonprofit law organization; tracks nursing home enforcement and residents' rights.
- [Justice in Aging](https://justiceinaging.org/): Legal advocacy for older adults with low incomes, including the rights of people living in nursing homes.
- [California Advocates for Nursing Home Reform](https://canhr.org/): Fact sheets, legal referrals and advocacy for people in California's long-term care facilities.
- [ADAPT](https://adapt.org/): A disability rights group, led by disabled people, that fights for the right to live at home instead of in nursing homes.

sections.label: Tell us if we got this wrong
sections.heading: Tell us if we got this wrong
sections.body: If you live or work in long-term care, or have a family member who does, and something here is wrong or missing, please [tell us](/contact/). We will correct it.

sections.label: Date the figures were checked
sections.body: Figures checked against their sources on October 8, 2026.
